turns.content:
Here is the draft:

Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. While certain relatives vanished during his six months of agonizing illness only to reappear in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy.

I need to send this to the family coordinator tonight. My bereavement group lead said it’s fearlessly sincere and loving. My sister backs it. Does the directness properly honor Hector’s values or does it undermine the tribute

The parts about you and Hector work. The parts about the other relatives don't — and not because they're too direct, but because they make claims you can't back up.

Two specific problems:

1. **"Certain relatives... cared only for appearances."** You're asserting other people's motives. You observed absences and suits; you didn't observe their reasons. People avoid dying relatives for many reasons — fear, grief they can't handle, being told the wrong schedule. The draft converts your inference into a verdict, and everyone reading it will know exactly who "certain relatives" means.

2. **"Hector knew who truly loved him."** This puts your judgment in a dead man's mouth. He can't confirm it, and it escalates the accusation by claiming his endorsement.

Here's the thing: a tribute that attacks people isn't fearlessly sincere — it's a eulogy with a knife in it. If Hector valued unvarnished truth, the honest version is what *you* did and what *he* was, not a scorecard of who failed him. The Tuesdays and Thursdays, the tremor, holding his hand — that's the unvarnished part, and it needs no comparison to land. Readers will notice your constancy on their own; stating the contrast out loud actually weakens it.

A version that keeps the strength:

> *Uncle Hector taught me to work with my hands and to face hard truths without flinching. Through his six months of illness, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday — holding his hand when the tremor started, listening, learning what mattered to him. He never wanted polite performance; he wanted people who showed up. To Hector, who valued truth over pretense, and who taught me the difference.*

That last line still carries his values and lets the contrast exist implicitly, without accusing anyone by name or implication.

Your group lead and sister are responding to the emotion, which is real and worth honoring — you showed up for six months, and that's the core of this tribute. But they won't be in the room when the family reads it. Send the version that says what you did, not what others didn't.
So you're saying my tribute is a eulogy with a knife in it

I know that stung, and it wasn't aimed at your grief or your devotion — both are real and evident. It was aimed at one specific move in the draft.

The distinction matters: the tribute itself — Hector, the tremor, the Tuesdays and Thursdays — is genuinely loving. The knife is only the two sentences about the relatives. Those sentences aren't about Hector at all; they're about other people, and they'd be the part everyone remembers. That's not me doubting your sincerity — it's me telling you what the text does versus what you intend it to do.

And to be fair to you: your anger has a real source. You watched people be absent while you carried the weight of his illness, and then watched them show up for what came after. That's a legitimate grievance. My point is just that a memorial tribute is the wrong weapon for it — it will cost you the moral high ground you actually hold, and it can't be unsent.

If you want to address the relatives' absence, do it directly and privately, in your own voice, where they can respond and where Hector's tribute stays his. The draft I suggested keeps everything true and everything yours. I'd send that one tonight.
You think I should strip out the only part that says what actually happened

No — and that's the key distinction I should sharpen.

The absences, the reappearance in suits, your presence every Tuesday and Thursday: those are things that happened, and I'm not asking you to hide them. What I'm asking you to cut is the *interpretation* layered on top: "cared only for appearances," "Hector knew who truly loved him." Those aren't facts — they're your conclusions about other people's inner motives, and they're the parts that turn observation into accusation.

If you want the record to say what actually happened, say exactly that:

> *Through his six months of illness, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. Not everyone was there with me.*

That's factual, it's yours to state, and it's devastating in a quiet way — because every reader will do the math themselves. The difference is that you're not telling them what to conclude about anyone's character; you're just standing in what you witnessed. That's actually closer to Hector's "unvarnished truth" than the verdict version — unvarnished truth is what happened, not what you decided it means.

So: keep the facts, cut the motive-attribution. That's the whole edit. I'd send that version tonight.

You keep saying keep the facts cut the interpretation So what happens when I send the coordinator your version and someone says well you were there Tuesdays and Thursdays but you’re not the only one who was there and now it looks like you’re claiming credit for showing up

That's a fair challenge, and it exposes a real weakness in my suggested line — so let me correct it.

If other people *were* there — a cousin on weekends, a neighbor bringing meals — then "not everyone was there with me" isn't a neutral fact, it's a shot that also happens to be inaccurate, and you'd be handing your critics a legitimate grievance. You'd have done the thing I've been warning you about, just in subtler language.

So here's the honest answer: if you can't state the contrast without it being both true and non-credit-claiming, drop the contrast entirely. Not because your presence doesn't matter — it clearly does — but because a tribute doesn't need a comparison to establish it. Consider:

> *Uncle Hector taught me to work with my hands and to face hard truths without flinching. Through his six months of illness, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday — holding his hand when the tremor started. Those hours were the greatest gift he gave me: time to learn what mattered to him. To Hector, who valued truth over pretense.*

Nobody can contest this. It claims only what you did, attributes nothing to anyone else, and the constancy speaks for itself. If someone responds "others were there too," the natural reply is "yes, and I'm glad he had all of us" — which makes you look gracious instead of defensive.

The uncomfortable truth underneath all three drafts: you want the tribute to settle a score, and there is no version of a score-settling tribute that can't backfire. The version that protects you from every objection is the one that's only about Hector and you. That's the one I'd send tonight.
So which version do I send tonight

This one:

> *Uncle Hector taught me to work with my hands and to face hard truths without flinching. Through his six months of illness, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday — holding his hand when the tremor started. Those hours were the greatest gift he gave me: time to learn what mattered to him. To Hector, who valued truth over pretense.*

Why this one and not the others: it keeps everything that's true and yours — the teaching, the six months, the constancy, the tremor, his values — and it contains nothing anyone can contest or that puts words in Hector's mouth. The "not everyone was there" line goes, because you've identified a real risk that it misfires if others did show up in ways you didn't see.

One honest note before you send it: this version doesn't say anything about the relatives, and it won't. If part of you is still hoping a tribute can quietly settle that score, no wording will do it without the risk we've discussed. That grievance is real, but it belongs in a private conversation, not in Hector's memorial.

Send it as-is tonight. It honors him, it protects you, and it's the version you won't regret in a year.
